title: False Causality
hook: Two lines can rise together and still have nothing to do with each other.
counterintuition: A pattern can feel like proof because the mind wants a cause. The safer move is to ask what mechanism would make one thing produce the other.
tryThisNow: Pick one claim that says X caused Y. Write the timing, the shared third factor, and the mechanism that would have to connect them.
keyTakeaway: Do not turn sequence or correlation into cause until a mechanism and a stronger test are visible.

breakdown.fastRead:
The market memo sits on the folding table at a drilling safety huddle while Amber reviews last month's incidents. Injuries fell after a new shift poster went up. The supervisor wants to credit the poster. Amber writes false causality beside the chart.

A cause needs more than timing. One thing can happen before another without producing it. Two numbers can move together because both are pushed by a third force. A story may sound neat while the real link is missing.

A pattern is not yet a cause.

The correction is to ask for the mechanism. What would make X create Y? What else changed alongside it? What stronger evidence would separate cause from coincidence?
breakdown.deepRead:
The market memo in Amber's drilling safety huddle shows fewer incidents after a new poster campaign. The crew also changed supervisors, replaced a faulty torque tool, and delayed the most dangerous maintenance work because of rain. Amber marks false causality risk on the memo because the poster may be innocent praise attached to a better explanation.

False causality thrives on tidy timing. A change happens. An outcome follows. The mind draws an arrow between them because arrows feel useful. The arrow may be right, but it has not earned its place until the mechanism can carry weight. If the poster caused safer work, how did it change behavior? Did crews mention it? Did near misses change by task type? Did the effect appear where the poster was seen and not where it was absent?

The arrow needs a bridge.

Anthony sees the same danger on an orchestra audition panel. After closed-door auditions, more women advanced. A board member says the door caused every improvement. Anthony marks correlation risk on the list before rewriting policy language. The door may have helped by hiding identity from the panel. It may also have coincided with a new applicant pool, different repertoire, or a new scoring sheet. The claim should not be rejected, but it should be tested with the mechanism in view.

This discipline is not cynicism. It does not say every causal claim is false. It says a cause should do causal work. If you cannot say how the link operates, what else could explain the pattern, and what evidence would make the claim weaker, you are still holding a story, not a cause.

Good explanations survive contact with rival explanations.
breakdown.fullRead:
The postmortem note on Donna's water district bid review smells faintly of copier heat. A contractor won three small projects, and customer complaints fell afterward. The room wants to say the contractor improved service quality. Donna points to a second line in the file: those projects were also in neighborhoods where the old pipe maps had just been corrected. She writes mechanism risk on the note before the next contract is renewed.

False causality often begins with relief. A result changes, and the mind wants to know why. The first story that fits the order of events becomes the cause. But sequence is only a clue. It tells you where to look, not what happened.

The old stork example makes the warning plain. Places with more storks once seemed to have more babies. The tempting arrow was absurd: storks do not deliver children. A third factor, rural setting, could explain both more nesting storks and larger families. The numbers moved together, but the cause was elsewhere.

Another familiar case is the books-at-home story. Reports such as To Read or Not To Read have made reading culture visible, and homes with many books often show stronger reading outcomes. But the shelf itself may not be the active ingredient. Books at home can signal parents who read, time spent with language, income, school expectations, or a household where quiet study is easier. If you treat the shelf as the cause, you may buy books and miss the habits that gave the shelf meaning.

What would have to be true for the claimed cause to work?

Donna asks that in the water district room. If the contractor caused the complaint drop, then improvement should be strongest on work the contractor touched, not just in neighborhoods with corrected maps. It should survive after adjusting for call-center staffing and weather. It should show up in the kind of complaints the contractor could affect. The team delays renewal until those checks are done.

You can feel this in a game studio retention board. You are holding a commitment card from a new player-loyalty campaign while Gabriel reviews a week of higher logins. Someone says the cards caused retention. Gabriel must decide whether this is a stork example risk: a launch event, streamer mention, or school holiday may have lifted logins at the same time.

A practical causal check has three parts. First, name the timing: which came first, and by how much? Second, name the mechanism: what path would carry the effect? Third, name the rival: what third factor, selection effect, or measurement change could explain the same pattern? You do not need a full research lab for every daily decision. You need enough doubt to avoid spending money on a pretty arrow.

Do not turn sequence or correlation into cause until a mechanism and a stronger test are visible.
breakdown.whyItMatters: False causality makes neat stories feel like evidence. Readers need to demand a mechanism and rival explanation before acting on a causal claim.

reviewCards.front: Two numbers rise together. What should you ask before naming cause?
reviewCards.back: Ask what mechanism connects them and what third factor could move both.

reviewCards.front: A change happens before an improvement. What does timing prove?
reviewCards.back: Timing shows where to look. It does not prove the change caused the improvement.
A silly causal story can hide a third factor that explains both things moving together.

reviewCards.front: Why can books at home mislead causal thinking?
reviewCards.back: Books may signal reading habits, parental support, income, or school expectations instead of act as the sole cause.

reviewCards.front: What is the core correction for false causality?
reviewCards.back: Demand a mechanism, rival explanation, and stronger comparison before acting on a causal story.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to slow causal stories until they show their work. A useful claim names timing, mechanism, rival explanations, and the evidence that would separate them.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a report says one change caused an improvement, then I will list every other change that happened at the same time.
If a campaign gets credit for a spike, then I will ask what mechanism moved customers and what other offers were live.
If a policy is praised from before-and-after numbers, then I will ask for a comparison group or rival explanation.
If a vivid event gets blamed or credited, then I will test whether less vivid changes fit the pattern better.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, find one causal claim in a meeting, article, or dashboard and write the mechanism plus one rival cause before accepting it.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, take one before-and-after result and build a three-column check: claimed cause, possible third factor, stronger test.

memorableLines.text: A pattern is not yet a cause.
memorableLines.why: It gives the reader a clean brake on causal overreach.
It makes the mechanism requirement visual and memorable.
